newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy rail head says derailed train was not faulty.
newsitem.headline: Italy rail head says derailed train was not faulty.

text.p: Italy's state railways said on Tuesday there appeared to be nothing wrong with a high-speed "Pendolino" train that derailed at the weekend, killing eight people on board, or the track it was travelling on.

Giancarlo Cimoli, the Ferrovie dello Stato (FS) managing director, told parliament that the stretch of track near Piacenza station where the train derailed conformed to specifications and signals were working correctly.
He said the ETR 460, made by FIAT, appeared on the basis of initial investigations to be "substantially intact" in its undercarriage, with "no evident damage" to the braking system or to the bogies.
The tilting system typical to the train, allowing it to lean into corners at speed and giving it its name which literally means "the pendulum", was also fully functional.
Authorities have focused on speed as a possible cause for the derailment of the train, Italy's fastest.
Unions and rail staff have rejected suggestions of human error, with two rail unions calling a two-hour strike for Thursday to draw attention to alleged safety problems.
The Milan to Rome train shot off the tracks as it approached Piacenza on Sunday afternoon.
The two drivers were among the eight dead and another 30 passengers were injured. Former Italian president Francesco Cossiga was on board but escaped unhurt.
Cimoli could not say what speed the train had been travelling at, explaning that the "black box" containing such technical details was still being held by investigating magistrates.
Piacenza's public prosecutor Alberto Grassi told a news conference on Tuesday no information would be given until the end of his inquiry.

In an unrelated incident, a 35-year-old man who was struck by a Rome-Turin "Pendolino" on Sunday while walking near the track outside the central Italian town of Montalto di Castro died of his injuries on Tuesday.
